prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realisation of the optical lattice clock, in which magic-wavelength trapping of neutral atoms allows many atoms to be interrogated in parallel and has brought optical frequency standards to the 10^-18 level of fractional uncertainty

statement.case_for: I keep the optical lattice clock as my preferred configuration after the full exchange, and the discussion has sharpened rather than weakened my reasons. The discovery is a specific principle: Katori's magic-wavelength lattice cancels the light shift of the trap on the clock transition while holding a large ensemble of neutral atoms free of Doppler and recoil shifts. Ye's group then showed what the principle could deliver, taking stability and accuracy to the 10^-18 level and into the many-body regime. This is not a conceptual extension of the 2005 comb prize or the 2012 single-ion prize. The comb solved the counting of optical cycles and the ion work solved control of one quantum system; the lattice clock solved how to interrogate many atoms at once without perturbing the transition, which is the step that changed the statistical limit of the measurement. The result has been reproduced and compared across several independent laboratories, and it already delivers measurable outcomes (constraints on constant variation, millimetre-scale gravitational redshift, searches for ultralight dark matter). On attribution this is the cleanest configuration on the shortlist: two names, a proposer and the leading realiser. Because the clock transitions depend on atomic polarisabilities and systematic-shift budgets that atomic theory has to supply, I can say with some confidence that the physical basis is sound. That is a statement about the atomic structure, not a judgement of the candidate's field-level importance.
statement.case_against: The most serious objection, raised by Danielsson, Mehlig, Pearce and Johansson, is that the scientific footprint is narrower than that of moire matter or topological phases, and that it sits in the lineage of the 2005 and 2012 prizes. I accept that the footprint is narrower in the sense that it yields few new phenomena, and I think this is a legitimate reason for some members to rank it lower. It is a measurement and invention achievement, not a new state of matter. A second weakness is the pending redefinition of the second: part of the practical significance is still prospective, and I cannot argue that it has been realised. Finally, the two names leave out Lemonde and the SYRTE work, the theorists of the magic-wavelength shifts, and the NIST and PTB ion-clock groups. I recall the priority history from memory, and I would want it checked against the published record before the citation is fixed.

responses.point: Pearce argues that B019 has the narrowest scientific footprint of the leading candidates, that the 2005 and 2012 prizes sit near it, and that the Nobel record often honours the decisive prediction and first observation while leaving the wider community out.
responses.response: I agree with the last point and it applies to B019 as well as to B012: with Katori and Ye the cut is at least a clean one. On footprint I partly concede. The lattice clock is not a new phase of matter. But footprint measured by new phenomena is not the only standard, and a precision measurement that tests constants and general relativity at the millimetre scale answers questions that no earlier clock could. On the overlap, the earlier prizes do not cover magic-wavelength trapping of neutral atoms; I would make the citation say so. Where we really differ is on what the committee should value, and I do not think a larger number of ranks for B012 settles that. I also still take the omission of Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang as the problem it is. It is a bigger gap than the one around Katori and Ye, even if it is defensible.

responses.point: Danielsson argues that the twisted-graphene discovery is concrete and reproduced, that an unsettled mechanism is a question about meaning and not about whether the discovery is real, and that Bistritzer must be credited.
responses.response: That is a fair point and it changed part of my view: I now accept that the unresolved pairing mechanism should not be treated as a bar by itself, because the discovery is the flat-band-driven correlated phases and not a finished explanation. I also accept that a citation can be built around the prediction and the observed phases. Where I still differ is the maturity of the quantitative comparison. Twist-angle disorder makes sample-to-sample comparison with the continuum model difficult, so the field has not yet shown the convergence of independent results that the lattice-clock community has shown for two decades. That is why B047 is my second alternative and my preferred configuration for a later year, not for this one. I agree with you and Olsson that the pre-2018 moire band-structure literature should be checked before the wording is fixed.

responses.point: Mehlig moved to B047 and says the attribution gap there is smaller than for B012, and also describes B019 as strong but a candidate for a later year or a partner in a two-part prize.
responses.response: I appreciate the clarification about my own B012 comment, and I agree that B047 has the smaller gap among the two. On your point about a two-part prize, I considered it. Pairing B019 with B047 or B012 would require splitting the three-name limit across parts, and nobody has made a case that the fields share a single idea. I do not think that combining two strong candidates for the sake of breadth is a scientific argument, so I keep a single part. I also do not accept that B019 is a case for a later year simply because the redefinition is pending: the demonstrated performance is what the discovery rests on, and the redefinition is a decision by metrology bodies, not a test of the physics.

responses.point: Olsson argues that the prize criterion is a discovery and not a finished explanation, and that replication across many groups and platforms since 2018 is the kind of confirmation the clock community points to.
responses.response: I agree on the criterion and I accept that replication of the 2018 phenomenology is real. My remaining reservation is narrower than the one I stated in round 1: reproduction of a phenomenon and agreement of independent results on a quantitative number are different things, and the lattice clocks have the second. Your microscopist's point about twist angle being directly measurable is persuasive, but local twist-angle variation within a device is also exactly what limits quantitative comparison. I would be more comfortable with B047 in a few years, and I would not regard it as an unreasonable outcome now.

responses.point: Kroll supports B019 and asked that the citation make clear why the lattice clock differs from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion prizes, and that priority between Katori, Ye and Lemonde be verified.
responses.response: I have tried to do this in the revised citation by naming the parallel interrogation of many neutral atoms in a magic-wavelength lattice as the point of the invention. On the priority history, I cannot verify it from the supplied material and I do not want either of us to settle it from memory. I would ask that the committee secretariat check the order of the first magic-wavelength proposal, the first strontium lattice-clock demonstration, and the SYRTE contributions before the citation is final. Since both of us work close to atomic and optical physics, I would also weigh the objections from condensed-matter colleagues on footprint carefully and not dismiss them.

responses.point: Johansson moved to B012, argues that Kane and Mele made the decisive conceptual step and that the 2016 prize does not cover the Z2 invariant, while conceding that the attribution is the real weakness.
responses.response: I find your argument that B012 is a separate discovery from the 2016 prize convincing, and I would no longer treat the 2016 prize as a bar. The attribution problem is the point that decides it for me. A citation that says prediction and first observation has to name those who made the prediction that the experiment tested, and I cannot reconcile that with leaving out Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang. If the committee can draft a wording that credits the Z2 proposal and the first HgTe observation and nothing more, I would support B012 as a good outcome, and it remains my first alternative.

uncertainties: Priority history between Katori, Ye and Lemonde and others (first magic-wavelength proposal, first strontium lattice-clock demonstration, early SYRTE work) is from memory and should be checked.

Whether the committee reads the lattice clock as a new principle distinct from the 2005 and 2012 prizes, or as a continuation. This depends on the wording of the citation and on a judgement of the field that members may reasonably disagree about.
Whether the footprint of B019 is sufficient compared with moire matter or topological phases. I have no way to settle this from within atomic physics.
Whether B012 can be given a fair citation given Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang, and whether B047 will settle in interpretation soon; I cannot resolve either from my own field.
statement.conflict_note: My documented connections (Lindgren's Gothenburg group, L'Huillier and the Lund attosecond group, Keller's group at ETH Zurich, Schuch, Dahlstrom, Argenti, Indelicato) do not include Katori or Ye, and none of the candidates in the preferred configuration or the alternatives involves attribution to them. I work as a theoretical atomic physicist in an adjacent area, which I disclose as field proximity, and I have no collaboration with the credited names. If the committee turns to attosecond science or highly charged ions, my collaborations with L'Huillier's and Keller's groups would require disclosure and possible recusal. No change since round 1.
